project.name: treetracker-wallet-app
project.description: Treetracker Wallet App is a secure digital token wallet platform built by Greenstand for transparent, verifiable tree-planting and forest-management token transfers. It is a Yarn v4 monorepo with a Next.js web app, an Expo React Native mobile app, and a NestJS backend, plus shared TypeScript packages.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: The README introduces the Treetracker Wallet App: a secure digital token wallet platform by Greenstand for transparent tree-planting and forest-management token transfers. It lays out the Yarn v4 monorepo layout, with apps/ (bdd, native, user, web) and packages/ (common, config, core, keycloak, queue, wallet), and gives quick-start instructions for Node.js, Yarn, and Docker. This is your map for the rest of the tour.

tour.title: Monorepo Workspace Structure
tour.description: The root package.json defines the Yarn v4 workspace that ties the whole project together, declaring apps/* and packages/* as workspaces and aggregating scripts to run, build, and test every app from one place. This single manifest is why three independently-runnable apps (web, native, backend) can share code and tooling without duplicating dependencies.
tour.languageLesson: Yarn workspaces let multiple packages live in one repository and reference each other by name (for example @treetracker/wallet) without publishing to a registry, while still hoisting shared dependencies to a single node_modules.

tour.title: Web App Entry Point
tour.description: apps/web/src/app/layout.tsx is the root Next.js layout wrapping every page in the web app. It wires up the MUI cache provider, the app theme, and a Keycloak auth provider, so any page rendered inside it already has access to styling and authentication. The keycloak.ts utility it depends on wraps a single browser-only Keycloak instance and exposes idempotent init, login, register, and logout helpers used throughout the app's auth pages.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js App Router layouts wrap all nested routes automatically; a root layout.tsx is the one file every page in the tree passes through, making it the natural place to inject cross-cutting providers.

tour.title: Native App Entry Point
tour.description: apps/native/app/_layout.tsx is the Expo Router equivalent of the web's root layout: it loads custom fonts, manages the splash screen lifecycle, and wraps the whole app in a ModalProvider. From there, apps/native/app/index.tsx is the first route hit, checking AsyncStorage for onboarding and auth status before redirecting to onboarding, home, or login. Comparing this to Step 3 shows the same authentication concerns solved with native-specific APIs (AsyncStorage) instead of the browser session storage the web app uses.
tour.languageLesson: Expo Router uses file-based routing like Next.js: an underscore-prefixed _layout.tsx wraps its sibling routes, and folder names (including parenthesized route groups) become URL segments.

tour.title: Backend Bootstrap
tour.description: apps/user/src/main.ts is the NestJS backend's bootstrap: it creates the app, configures Swagger docs, CORS, and global validation pipes, then starts listening. apps/app.module.ts is the root module it wires up, bringing together the user, queue-listener, and auth modules. Together they show how the backend service, the third runnable app in this monorepo, assembles its dependency graph at startup.
tour.languageLesson: NestJS organizes code into modules, each declaring the providers and controllers it owns; the root module composes feature modules together, similar to dependency injection containers in other server frameworks.

tour.title: Shared Auth State (Jotai Core Package)
tour.description: packages/core holds the Jotai-based state shared by both the web and native apps. Its auth atoms (loginAtom, registerAtom, logoutAtom, tokenAtom) implement the actual login/register/logout logic against the treetracker auth API, while tokenAtom persists the resulting token behind a cross-platform storage adapter, session storage on web, AsyncStorage on native. This is the piece that lets Steps 3 and 4's auth providers behave identically across platforms.
tour.languageLesson: Jotai atoms are small, composable units of state; a write-only atom (like loginAtom) performs a side effect and updates other atoms, while a persisted atom serializes its value to storage so state survives reloads.

tour.title: Wallet API Client Package
tour.description: packages/wallet is the shared library both frontends use to talk to the wallet backend. Its barrel file re-exports typed API client functions (createWallet, getWallets) and matching React hooks (useCreateWallet, useGetWallets) built on the Wallet, Transfer, and Transaction types. This package's high fan-in across the codebase makes it one of the most depended-upon modules, both apps' wallet, token, and transfer screens are built on top of it.

tour.title: Keycloak Integration
tour.description: Authentication is centralized around Keycloak, and packages/keycloak provides the shared client functions (fetchTokenFromKeycloak, createAccountFromKeycloak, deleteAccountFromKeycloak) used outside the browser. On the backend, apps/user/src/auth/auth.service.ts uses the same client-credentials flow to obtain a cached service-account token, which apps/user/src/user/user.service.ts then uses to call Keycloak's admin REST API for login, registration, and profile lookups. This is the trust boundary connecting Step 3's browser login to real user records.

tour.title: Event-Driven Wallet Creation (Queue Package)
tour.description: packages/queue is a small Postgres-based pub/sub client, its barrel file re-exports just subscribe and publish. The backend's queue-listener module uses it to subscribe to a wallet-creation notification channel: apps/user/src/queue-listener/queue-listener.service.ts triggers on module init and forwards each new account to downstream processing. This decouples user registration (Step 8) from whatever needs to react to a new wallet being created.

tour.title: Web App: Wallet and Transfer Screens
tour.description: With the shared packages in place, the web app's protected routes show them composed into real UI. The home page displays wallet and token balances from Step 7's hooks, the wallet page drives wallet creation including duplicate-name checks and pending shared-token redemption, and the send page implements the full transfer flow: choose a wallet, enter a recipient and amount, and submit. These routes only render once Step 3's auth layout confirms a valid session.

tour.title: Native App: Wallet and Transfer Screens
tour.description: The native app mirrors the web app's core flows using the same packages/wallet and packages/core foundations from Steps 6 and 7. The home tab renders balance cards and recent activity, the wallet tab lists wallets with a create-wallet drawer, and the transfer entry screen collects a token amount and note before proceeding. Comparing this to Step 10 highlights how the shared packages let two very different UI frameworks, Next.js and Expo Router, stay behaviorally consistent.

tour.title: End-to-End BDD Testing
tour.description: The apps/bdd workspace validates the whole system from a user's point of view using Cucumber and WebdriverIO. Feature files like send-token.feature describe transfer scenarios (accepting, declining, cancelling a pending transfer) in plain-language Gherkin, and steps.ts implements the Given/When/Then handlers that drive the actual web app UI from Steps 3 and 10 while seeding test data through the wallet API from Step 7.
tour.languageLesson: Gherkin's Given/When/Then syntax separates the readable specification (the .feature file) from its implementation (the step-definitions file), letting non-engineers review test coverage without reading code.

tour.title: Containerizing and Deploying the Backend
tour.description: The backend service is packaged with a multi-stage Dockerfile: a builder stage installs dependencies and compiles the NestJS app from Step 5, then a minimal Alpine production stage copies only the compiled dist and runtime node_modules, exposing port 8080. The Kubernetes Deployment manifest then runs two replicas of that image, pinned to the microservices node pool, giving the backend production redundancy.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds keep dev-only tooling (compilers, dev dependencies) out of the final image by copying just the build artifacts into a fresh, minimal base image, shrinking the production footprint.

tour.title: CI/CD Pipelines
tour.description: GitHub Actions workflows tie everything together as a capstone. pr-ci-cd-all.yml runs on every PR across the whole repo, checking Prettier formatting, lint-staged, and commit message conventions, while ci-cd-deploy-web-prod.yml is a manually-triggered pipeline that builds the Next.js web app from Step 3 as a static export and deploys it to production behind CloudFront. Together with the per-app pipelines not shown here, these pipelines enforce the quality bar and automate the deployment path from source to production for all three apps.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows are triggered by an 'on' block (push, pull_request, or workflow_dispatch for manual runs), organize work into parallel 'jobs', and each job runs sequential 'steps'.
